```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.5,
                      fig.height = 4.2, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 100)
```

A variable-order transition tree is a probabilistic model of the next state
given the states that preceded it. For every history it selects the longest
suffix that the tree holds as a context and returns that context's next-state
distribution (Ron, Singer and Tishby, 1996; Bühlmann and Wyner, 1999). The
same distribution serves several purposes. It predicts what comes next. It
assigns a likelihood to an observed sequence, so sequences and single
transitions can be ranked by how expected or surprising they are, and so a
model can be judged by the probability it gives to sequences it has not seen.
It generates new sequences, and it fills gaps in incomplete ones.

This guide covers these uses: `predict()` and `query_pathway()` for the next
state, `perplexity()` and `model_fit()` for held-out fit, `score_sequences()`,
`score_positions()` and `plot_predictive()` for scoring, `mine_sequences()`
and `mine_contexts()` for finding unusual sequences and contexts,
`generate_sequences()` and `simulate()` for generation, and
`impute_sequences()` for gaps.

## Data

`engagement` holds the engagement states of 1,000 students over 25 time
steps.

- **Sequence:** one row per student.
- **Time:** columns `T1` to `T25`; `NA` marks positions after a student
  dropped out.
- **State:** `Active`, `Average` or `Disengaged`.

The first 800 students are used to fit the tree and the last 200 are held
out to evaluate it. `head()` and `tail()` split the rows.

```{r data}
library(transitiontrees)
dim(engagement)
training <- head(engagement, 800)
held_out <- tail(engagement, 200)
```

## The model

To fit the tree, we call `context_tree()` with `max_depth` for the longest
history and `min_count` for the smallest number of observations a context
needs; `prune_tree()` then removes contexts whose prediction does not differ
from their parent's by the $G^2$ test.

```{r fit}
grown <- context_tree(training, max_depth = 3L, min_count = 10L)
tree <- prune_tree(grown)
tree
```

Of the 40 contexts grown, pruning keeps 6. One step of history carries most
of the information: only two contexts of depth two survive,
`Disengaged -> Average` and `Average -> Disengaged`, and none of depth three.
The pathway notation reads oldest to newest, so `Disengaged -> Average` is a
student who was disengaged and is now average.

## Predicting the next state

To predict the next state after one or more histories, we call `predict()`
with `newdata` for the histories and `tidy = TRUE` for one row per history.
Each history is a character vector of states, oldest first.

```{r predict}
histories <- list(c("Active", "Active"),
                  c("Disengaged", "Average"),
                  c("Average", "Average", "Disengaged"))
predict(tree, newdata = histories, tidy = TRUE)
```

`history` is the history as given and `context` the longest suffix of it that
the tree holds, from which the prediction is made. The first history backs off
from `Active -> Active` to `Active`, because pruning removed the longer
context; the third backs off to `Average -> Disengaged`. `predicted` is the most likely
next state, `probability` its probability, and the last three columns give the
full distribution. A student who was disengaged and is now average stays
average with probability 0.57, becomes active with probability 0.32 and
returns to disengagement with probability 0.11.

To obtain only the predicted states, we set `type = "class"`.

```{r predict-class}
predict(tree, newdata = histories, type = "class")
```

## Querying a pathway

To read the distribution of one context, we call `query_pathway()` with the
pathway. A pathway the tree does not hold backs off to its longest held
suffix, as in `predict()`.

```{r query}
query_pathway(tree, c("Disengaged", "Average"))
```

To obtain the probability of one next state, we add `next_state`.

```{r query-state}
query_pathway(tree, "Disengaged", next_state = "Disengaged")
```

To refuse back-off and require the context itself, we set `exact = TRUE`; a
pathway the tree does not hold then returns `NA`. `pathway_exists()` answers
the same question with `TRUE` or `FALSE`.

```{r query-exact}
query_pathway(tree, c("Active", "Active"), exact = TRUE)
pathway_exists(tree, "Disengaged -> Average")
pathway_exists(tree, "Active -> Active")
```

## Held-out fit

Perplexity is the exponential of the average negative log-likelihood per
predicted state. It reads as the effective number of equally likely next
states the model is choosing between: a model that knows nothing about three
states has perplexity 3, and a model that is always certain and correct has
perplexity 1. To compute it on the training sequences and on the held-out
ones, we call `perplexity()` without and with `newdata`.

```{r perplexity}
perplexity(tree)
perplexity(tree, newdata = held_out)
perplexity(grown, newdata = held_out)
```

The pruned tree has perplexity 1.93 on the sequences it was fitted to and 1.96
on the held-out students, a small gap that shows little overfitting. The
unpruned tree, with 40 contexts instead of 6, predicts the held-out students
no better (1.96). To obtain the log-likelihood, degrees of freedom, number of
predicted states, AIC, BIC and perplexity in one row, we call `model_fit()`.

```{r model-fit}
model_fit(tree)
model_fit(tree, newdata = held_out)
```

The held-out row scores 5,000 transitions of the 200 students. The choice of
`max_depth`, `min_count`, smoothing and pruning by cross-validated perplexity
is covered in
[Model selection: tuning, fit and perplexity](model-selection.html).

## Scoring sequences

To score each held-out sequence, we call `score_sequences()`. Each row is one
sequence: `n_scored` is the number of states predicted, `log_lik` the summed
natural-log probability of the observed states and `perplexity` the
sequence's own perplexity.

```{r score-sequences}
sequence_scores <- score_sequences(tree, newdata = held_out)
head(sequence_scores)
summary(sequence_scores)
```

Most held-out students have a perplexity close to the model's 1.96; the
range runs from 1.30 to 2.87. To list the sequences the model finds most
surprising, we call `mine_sequences()` with `which = "surprising"` and `n`
for the number to return; `which = "expected"` returns the most predictable.

```{r mine-sequences}
mine_sequences(tree, newdata = held_out, which = "surprising", n = 5L)
mine_sequences(tree, newdata = held_out, which = "expected", n = 3L)
```

`sequence_id` is the row of `held_out`. The most surprising student, row 111,
has a perplexity of 2.87, close to the value of 3 for a model that knows
nothing; the most expected, row 99, has 1.30.

## Scoring positions

To score every transition, we call `score_positions()`. Each row is one
position of one sequence, with the context used for the prediction, the
observed state, the probability the tree gave it and its log-probability.

```{r score-positions}
position_scores <- score_positions(tree, newdata = held_out)
head(position_scores)
```

To list the least expected transitions, we set `worst` to the number to
return.

```{r score-worst}
score_positions(tree, newdata = held_out, worst = 5L)
```

The least expected transitions are all a jump from `Disengaged` straight to
`Active`, which the tree gives a probability of 0.049.

## Plotting predictive performance

To see where in a sequence the model is uncertain, we call `plot_predictive()`
with `type = "logloss"`. Each point is one transition's log-loss
$-\log_2 P(\text{observed})$ in bits; the line follows the mean at each
position.

```{r plot-logloss}
plot_predictive(tree, newdata = held_out, type = "logloss")
```

To see the distribution of the probabilities given to the observed states, we
set `type = "ecdf"`. A curve that rises late belongs to a model that gives
high probability to what happens.

```{r plot-ecdf}
plot_predictive(tree, newdata = held_out, type = "ecdf")
```

Because the pruned tree has six contexts, each giving one probability to
each of the three states, the scored probabilities take at most 18 distinct
values, and the curve rises in steps.

To follow individual sequences, we set `type = "position"`. The view is
readable for a few sequences, so we pass the first five held-out students.

```{r plot-position}
plot_predictive(tree, newdata = head(held_out, 5), type = "position")
```

## Mining contexts

To find the contexts in which a state is likely, we call `mine_contexts()`
with `state` and `min_prob`.

```{r mine-contexts}
mine_contexts(tree, state = "Disengaged", min_prob = 0.5)
```

Disengagement is the most likely next state after `Disengaged` (0.79) and
after `Average -> Disengaged` (0.74). To find the contexts in which a state
is unlikely, we use `max_prob`.

```{r mine-contexts-low}
mine_contexts(tree, state = "Active", max_prob = 0.1)
```

A student who was disengaged at the last step becomes active at the next step with
probability 0.05 to 0.06.

## Generating sequences

A fitted tree is a generative model: walking forward and drawing each state
from the distribution of the current context produces new sequences. To
generate sequences, we call `generate_sequences()` with `n` for the number,
`length` for their length and `tidy = TRUE` for a wide data frame with one row
per sequence.

```{r generate}
set.seed(1)
generate_sequences(tree, n = 4L, length = 10L, tidy = TRUE)
```

To fix the first state of each sequence, we pass one state per sequence to
`start`.

```{r generate-start}
generate_sequences(tree, n = 3L, length = 8L,
                   start = c("Active", "Average", "Disengaged"), tidy = TRUE)
```

`simulate()` is the standard R generic for the same draw; its `seed` argument
makes the result reproducible without setting the global seed.

```{r simulate}
simulate(tree, nsim = 4L, seed = 42L, length = 10L, tidy = TRUE)
```

Simulated sequences can be compared with the data the tree was fitted to. To
compare the state frequencies, we simulate 800 sequences of 25 states, fit a
tree to them, and call `state_frequencies()` on both trees.

```{r simulate-check}
simulated <- simulate(tree, nsim = 800L, seed = 1L, length = 25L, tidy = TRUE)
state_frequencies(context_tree(simulated, max_depth = 1L))
state_frequencies(tree)
```

The proportions agree to within two percentage points (for example, 0.528
`Active` in the simulated sequences and 0.510 in the training data). The
simulated sequences have no dropout, so their totals differ.

## Imputing gaps

To fill internal gaps in incomplete sequences, we call `impute_sequences()`.
Each missing state is predicted from the longest held context of the states
before it, left to right, so an imputed state becomes part of the history for
later gaps. Trailing `NA`s, which mark the end of a sequence, are left as
they are. `method = "modal"` fills with the most likely state.

```{r impute}
gappy <- data.frame(T1 = c("Active", "Average", "Disengaged"),
                    T2 = c("Active", NA, "Disengaged"),
                    T3 = c(NA, "Average", NA),
                    T4 = c("Disengaged", "Disengaged", "Average"),
                    T5 = c("Disengaged", NA, NA))
impute_sequences(tree, newdata = gappy, method = "modal")
```

The trailing `NA`s in `T5` remain. To sample each gap from the predicted
distribution instead, we set `method = "prob"` with a `seed`; repeated draws
with different seeds give multiple imputations.

```{r impute-prob}
impute_sequences(tree, newdata = gappy, method = "prob", seed = 1L)
impute_sequences(tree, newdata = gappy, method = "prob", seed = 2L)
```

Modal imputation fills each gap with the single most likely state and so
understates the variability of the data; sampled imputation keeps it.

## Summary

| Question | Call |
|---|---|
| What comes next after these histories? | `predict(tree, newdata, tidy = TRUE)` |
| The predicted state only | `predict(tree, newdata, type = "class")` |
| The distribution after one pathway | `query_pathway(tree, pathway)` |
| Does the tree hold this context? | `pathway_exists(tree, pathway)` |
| How well does the model predict new sequences? | `perplexity(tree, newdata)`, `model_fit(tree, newdata)` |
| How expected is each sequence? | `score_sequences(tree, newdata)` |
| The most surprising sequences | `mine_sequences(tree, newdata, which = "surprising")` |
| How expected is each transition? | `score_positions(tree, newdata, worst = 5L)` |
| Where is the model uncertain? | `plot_predictive(tree, newdata, type = "logloss")` |
| In which contexts is a state likely? | `mine_contexts(tree, state, min_prob = 0.5)` |
| New sequences from the model | `simulate(tree, nsim, seed, length, tidy = TRUE)` |
| Fill gaps | `impute_sequences(tree, newdata, method = "modal")` |
